title: The AI cloud is heading into the vault. CoreWeave is taking it to the spies.

content_html:
The AI cloud is heading into the vault. CoreWeave rents high-end GPUs to the biggest AI labs. Now it wants to run that same cloud inside the sealed facilities where America keeps its secrets, with the contractor Leidos as its guide.

The two companies announced the collaboration on Thursday. CoreWeave will place its AI platform inside Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities, the sealed rooms known as SCIFs where classified intelligence is stored and analysed. Leidos will handle the parts a commercial cloud provider cannot: accreditation, secure architecture, cyber operations and mission integration.

The customers are America’s spy agencies and the Department of War, as the Pentagon is now styled. Both sides call it “sovereign” AI capacity. It is the same stack CoreWeave rents to commercial labs, rebuilt to the rules that classified work demands.

What they plan to sell

The two companies sketched out five things they intend to offer. There is a classified cloud for training and running models, plus tools to help analysts fuse intelligence, exploit imagery and reach decisions.

The rest leans into security and simulation. There are cyber ranges to war-game AI attacks, plus synthetic data and digital twins for training. A final piece links the central cloud to disconnected, forward-deployed units in the field.

Sachin Jain, CoreWeave’s chief operating officer, said federal teams need “secure, scalable platforms” to put AI to work. He said the company wants to extend the tools it gives the world’s top AI labs “to highly secure government environments.”

Why accreditation is the hard part

The constraint here is not chips. It is clearance. A commercial AI cloud is built for the opposite of secrecy: huge shared regions, elastic capacity, customers reaching their clusters over the open internet.

Classified work needs the reverse. The hardware has to sit in a facility cleared for the data, run by cleared staff and cut off from the public internet. Auditing and model governance come built in, not bolted on.

That gap is why a government cannot simply rent a slice of an ordinary cloud region. It is also why an integrator like Leidos is in the deal at all.

Leidos brings the scale for that work. It reported about $17.2bn in revenue last year and employs more than 50,000 people. “This is the next evolution of mission technology,” said Jason O’Connor, president of Leidos Intelligence, describing “sovereign AI compute at scale, secure by design.”

Why CoreWeave needs the work

For CoreWeave, federal money solves a specific problem: concentration. The company grew explosively by renting compute to a handful of giants. It reported $2.08bn in first-quarter revenue, up 112% on the year, against a backlog worth $99.4bn.

Much of that rests on a few names, including a $21bn commitment from Meta and a multi-year deal with Anthropic. Selling to spies and soldiers spreads that risk.

It also fits a wider push. CoreWeave launched a dedicated federal arm last year, aligning with FedRAMP and other government sign-offs. Rivals are chasing the same budgets. Those include military cyber startups and chipmakers handing supercomputers to the armed forces.

Washington is also consolidating its software contracts, and the hunt for sovereign AI now stretches well beyond it, from Europe’s own military-AI push onward.

What is actually signed

Not much yet. CoreWeave’s own filing notes the arrangement depends on definitive agreements that are not yet signed. It says deployment will follow “mission requirements and federal appropriation priorities.” In plain terms, this moves at the speed of Washington, not the speed of a commercial contract.

The capacity is there to draw on. CoreWeave passed 1GW of active power in the first quarter and has contracted more than 3.5GW. Its chief executive, Michael Intrator, says it is heading toward more than 8GW by 2030.

The classified slice will be tiny by comparison. It is limited less by megawatts than by where an accredited rack can legally sit.

content_html_zh:
人工智能云正在进入金库。 CoreWeave 向最大的人工智能实验室出租高端 GPU。 现在，它希望在美国保守秘密的密封设施内运行同样的云，并以承包商 Leidos 为指导。

两家公司于周四宣布了合作。 CoreWeave 将把其人工智能平台放置在敏感隔离信息设施内，即被称为 SCIF 的密封房间，其中存储和分析机密情报。 Leidos 将处理商业云提供商无法处理的部分：认证、安全架构、网络运营和任务集成。

客户是美国的间谍机构和战争部（五角大楼现在的风格）。 双方都称其为“主权”人工智能能力。 这与 CoreWeave 租给商业实验室的堆栈相同，并按照分类工作需求的规则进行了重建。

他们计划出售什么

两家公司概述了他们打算提供的五项内容。 有一个用于训练和运行模型的分类云，以及帮助分析师融合情报、利用图像和做出决策的工具。

其余的则侧重于安全和模拟。 有用于战争游戏人工智能攻击的网络靶场，还有用于训练的合成数据和数字孪生。 最后一部分将中央云与现场断开的、前沿部署的单元连接起来。

CoreWeave 首席运营官 Sachin Jain 表示，联邦团队需要“安全、可扩展的平台”来让人工智能发挥作用。 他表示，该公司希望将其为世界顶级人工智能实验室提供的工具扩展到“高度安全的政府环境”。

为什么认证是困难的部分

这里的限制不是芯片。 是清关。 商业人工智能云的构建与保密相反：巨大的共享区域、弹性容量、客户通过开放互联网访问其集群。

机密工作则需要相反。 硬件必须安装在数据清理完毕的设施中，由清理完毕的工作人员运行，并与公共互联网隔绝。 审计和模型治理是内置的，而不是附加的。

这种差距就是政府不能简单地租用普通云区域的一部分的原因。 这也是像 Leidos 这样的集成商参与此次交易的原因。

Leidos 为这项工作带来了规模。 该公司去年的营收约为 172 亿美元，员工超过 50,000 人。 Leidos Intelligence 总裁杰森·奥康纳 (Jason O’Connor) 表示：“这是任务技术的下一代发展。”他描述了“大规模的主权人工智能计算，设计安全。”

为什么 CoreWeave 需要这项工作

对于 CoreWeave 来说，联邦资金解决了一个具体问题：集中度。 该公司通过向少数巨头出租计算能力而实现爆炸式增长。 该公司公布第一季度营收 20.8 亿美元，同比增长 112%，而积压订单价值 994 亿美元。

其中大部分取决于几个名字，包括 Meta 的 210 亿美元承诺以及与 Anthropic 的多年协议。 向间谍和士兵出售产品会分散这种风险。

它还适合更广泛的推动。 CoreWeave 去年成立了一个专门的联邦机构，与 FedRAMP 和其他政府签署的协议保持一致。 竞争对手正在追求相同的预算。 其中包括军事网络初创公司和向武装部队提供超级计算机的芯片制造商。

华盛顿也在整合其软件合同，而对主权人工智能的追求现在远远超出了这一范围，从欧洲自己的军事人工智能的推动开始。

实际签署的是什么

还没有多少。 CoreWeave 自己的文件指出，该安排取决于尚未签署的最终协议。 它表示部署将遵循“任务要求和联邦拨款优先事项”。 简单来说，这一切以华盛顿的速度进行，而不是商业合同的速度。

能力是可以利用的。 CoreWeave第一季度的活跃发电量超过1GW，签约量超过3.5GW。 其首席执行官 Michael Intrator 表示，到 2030 年，该公司的目标是超过 8GW。

相比之下，分类的切片会很小。 其受兆瓦的限制小于经认可的机架可以合法放置的位置的限制。
